Using GRPO on approximately 440K ReSynth questions, with no real images during training, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B improve by 17.73 and 6.10 average points on BLINK, MUIRBench, and VLM2-Bench, while single-image performance is broadly preserved on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and improves across all four evaluated benchmarks on Qwen3-VL-8B. Notably, this supervision enables the 8B perception model itself to outperform Qwen3-VL-235B on BLINK and MUIRBench.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: WaveView: The Novel View Is in the Noise
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Generative novel view synthesis (NVS) employs a diffusion model to render a static or dynamic scene from a target camera view. Explicit warp methods complete a reprojection of the source with video diffusion models, and implicit methods encode the camera parameters or 3D cues. Both add inference overhead, and the generated layout often drifts from the ground truth. We present WaveView, which injects the warped source into the phase of the initial noise of a pretrained generator. The Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Packet Transform (DT-CWPT) allows local and anisotropic phase injection. The generator is thus constrained less in disoccluded regions and along the epipolar line. WaveView keeps the architecture and adds negligible overhead. On the DL3DV benchmark, it outperforms all baselines in every overlap bin. In the hardest bin, it gains 0.84 dB PSNR on the covisible region over MetaView, which shares its generator, while running 2.1 times faster. For dynamic NVS, fine-tuning AnyView with the same noise raises its zero-shot PSNR on AnyViewBench from 11.58 to 12.35 dB.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SIRAZ: Sparse Inter-Layer Residual Aggregation for Zero-Shot Visual Neural Decoding
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Brain-computer interfaces aim to establish direct communication between neural activity and external systems, making interpretation of brain signals an important problem. In this context, neural visual decoding seeks to infer visual information from neural activity by learning a mapping between brain responses and the corresponding visual stimuli. It investigates how visual information emerges from neural signals and relates to perceptual processing while enabling the reconstruction or retrieval of visual stimuli from neural signals. Our brain primarily follows a hierarchical pathway to process visual information captured by the eye. However, neural representations learned by existing methods differ fundamentally from those produced by the biological visual system. To bridge this gap and mimic the human vision hierarchy, we introduce Sparse Inter-layer Residual Aggregation for Zero-shot (SIRAZ). SIRAZ is a framework that aligns neural visual representations by jointly modeling early visual processes via fovea- and magnocellular-pathway-inspired Difference-of-Gaussians transformations. To align the semantic information with neural information, it extracts multiple intermediate representations of the image at multiple depths and passes them through the Residual Gated Adapter Mechanism. To study the temporal dynamics of neural signals, the Direction-aware Multi-Scale Temporal Attention Encoder is introduced to align the learned neural representation with the final visual representation. The proposed framework achieves 92.5% top-1 and 99.27% top-5 accuracy in the intra-subject setting on the THINGS-EEG dataset, and 50.25% and 75% top-1 and top-5 accuracy in the THINGS-MEG dataset. The results indicate that combining biologically motivated visual representations with the structured modalities of neural dynamics improves cross-modal alignment and zero-shot image retrieval.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: EgoGeneralist: Unifying Egocentric Action-Video Tasks through Video-Native Modeling
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Modern video models possess strong visual priors, yet do not natively represent human action in metric 3D space. We present EgoGeneralist, which adapts pretrained video generators to unify action-conditioned video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation for egocentric manipulation. Our role-adaptive action renderer provides video-native representations for multidirectional action-video learning, making metric motion usable as both a spatial control signal and a recoverable generation target. Cross-stream action-video coupling establishes close correspondence between metric motion and visual dynamics through lightweight adaptation while preserving the pretrained visual prior. Together, these designs establish a generalist framework spanning six action-video tasks. With only narrow-domain data, EgoGeneralist generalizes to diverse unseen scenes and interactions with effective action control and visual quality, bridging pretrained visual knowledge and metric 3D human motion.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CausalSpatial: A Benchmark for Object-Centric Causal Spatial Reasoning
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Humans can look at a static scene and instantly predict what happens next -- will moving this object cause a collision? We call this ability Causal Spatial Reasoning. However, current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot do this, as they remain largely restricted to static spatial perception, struggling to answer "what-if" questions in a 3D scene. We introduce CausalSpatial, a diagnostic benchmark evaluating whether models can anticipate consequences of object motions across four tasks: Collision, Compatibility, Occlusion, and Trajectory. Results expose a severe gap: humans score 84% while GPT-5 achieves only 54%. Why do MLLMs fail? Our analysis uncovers a fundamental deficiency: models over-rely on textual chain-of-thought reasoning that drifts from visual evidence, producing fluent but spatially ungrounded hallucinations. To address this, we propose the Causal Object World model (COW), a framework that externalizes the simulation process by generating videos of hypothetical dynamics. With explicit visual cues of causality, COW enables models to ground their reasoning in physical reality rather than linguistic priors. We make the dataset and code publicly available here: https://github.com/CausalSpatial/CausalSpatial

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Agreement Is Not Accuracy: LiDAR Elevation Errors Hidden in LiDAR-Camera Extrinsics
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: LiDAR and cameras provide complementary measurements for 3D vision, yet agreement between their observations does not establish the accuracy of either sensor's internal geometry. We show that systematic LiDAR elevation biases can be absorbed into the estimated extrinsics. Using synchronized LiDAR intensities and camera-estimated checkerboard poses, we jointly estimate a sensor-specific elevation correction shared across recordings and extrinsics for each recording. Ray-plane intersections locate the checker pattern without using reported ranges, preventing range errors from directly moving the lookup. Under matched intensity and correction models, this lookup gives smaller camera-consistency residuals than measured-point lookup. Across six identically designed rigs using the same sensor models, recording-excluded corrections reduce the mean translation-reference distance from 7.57 to 3.04 mm. On separate structures, they reduce inter-plane angle errors against references from independent dense camera scans and improve image-edge alignment. Rolling the rigs shifts the plane pairs exhibiting the largest angular improvements, as predicted for an elevation-only correction. Within the ray-plane model, calibration-target projections and loop-consistency residuals change little despite these geometric improvements. These findings show why agreement after extrinsic calibration need not establish correct internal LiDAR geometry. Synchronized observations of a familiar checkerboard provide a practical route to estimating and testing elevation corrections without a dedicated large calibration field. We plan to release code and data for reproducing the main results.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: TOMAS: Topology-Aware Operation Modeling and Adaptive Staging for Egocentric Hand Forecasting
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Forecasting future hand movements from egocentric videos plays an important role in understanding human intentions and hand-object interactions. However, different manipulation intentions can lead to substantially different hand trajectories even when interacting with the same object. Existing methods have not sufficiently explored the intrinsic relationships between articulated hand movements and object semantics to capture such operation-dependent motion patterns. Therefore, we propose TOMAS, a topology-aware operation modeling and adaptive staging framework for egocentric hand forecasting. Specifically, we develop a topology-aware hand-object reasoning mechanism that associates hand skeletal structures and articulation dynamics with object semantics and spatial relationships to jointly infer potential interaction targets and latent manipulation operations. The resulting object-operation representations provide interaction conditions for future hand trajectory prediction, with supervision adapted to the annotations available in each dataset. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive staging mechanism that organizes future hand movements into ordered latent stages with learnable temporal boundaries. Stage-specific geometric subgoals are then incorporated to guide trajectory refinement according to the underlying manipulation patterns. Experimental results on multiple publicly available benchmarks demonstrate that TOMAS achieves state-of-the-art performance in multi-dimensional and multi-target hand motion forecasting.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Dual-Manifold Variational Autoencoders
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: In latent diffusion models, expanding the latent dimension of variational autoencoders (VAEs) is essential to push the upper bound of reconstruction quality. However, without explicit structural constraints, such unregularized expansion easily yields a rugged and ill-conditioned latent manifold, causing generated latents to drift off the manifold during generation (i.e., off-manifold problem). Recent works smooth this manifold by using external foundation models (e.g., DINOv2) as a topological regularizer. However, we argue that tying the latent space to frozen external priors inherently restricts generalization: bound by their pre-training distributions and semantic biases, they may fail to capture faithful visual details on out-of-distribution domains. Observing that low-dimensional latents naturally form a smoother, generation-friendly manifold, we propose dual-manifold VAE (DM-VAE) to leverage internal representations as a topological regularizer. Specifically, DM-VAE pairs a high-dimensional reconstructive branch with a low-dimensional branch that extracts a clean topological skeleton, anchoring the high-dimensional manifold to this smooth subspace. Building upon this framework, we further introduce topological representation alignment (TRA) to supervise intermediate generator features during training, and internal guidance with topological skeleton (IG_TS) to guide structural components while preserving high-frequency details at inference. On ImageNet-1K (256x256), our foundation-model-free DM-VAE achieves a state-of-the-art rFID of 0.12 and a generation FID50K of 1.28 (w/o CFG) and 1.20 (w/CFG), and further reaches 1.11 when orthogonally combined with DINOv2.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Multimodal Information Fusion for Chart Understanding: A Survey of MLLMs -- Evolution, Limitations, and Cognitive Enhancement
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Chart understanding is a quintessential information fusion task, requiring the seamless integration of graphical and textual data to extract meaning. The advent of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has revolutionized this domain, yet the landscape of MLLM-based chart analysis remains fragmented and lacks systematic organization. This survey provides a comprehensive roadmap of this nascent frontier by structuring the domain's core components. We begin by analyzing the fundamental challenges of fusing visual and linguistic information in charts. We then categorize downstream tasks and datasets, introducing a novel taxonomy of canonical and non-canonical benchmarks to highlight the field's expanding scope. Subsequently, we present a comprehensive evolution of methodologies, tracing the progression from classic deep learning techniques to state-of-the-art MLLM paradigms that leverage sophisticated fusion strategies. By critically examining the limitations of current models, particularly their perceptual and reasoning deficits, we identify promising future directions, including advanced alignment techniques and reinforcement learning for cognitive enhancement. This survey aims to equip researchers and practitioners with a structured understanding of how MLLMs are transforming chart information fusion and to catalyze progress toward more robust and reliable systems.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: GRTO: Bootstrapped Group Relative Tool Optimization for Referring Segmentation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Referring segmentation requires reasoning to connect language with visual evidence and identify the intended target in challenging scenarios. This makes GRPO a natural choice for training VLMs together with a segmentation tool. However, existing approaches optimize only the VLM, assuming that the tool is perfect and leaving it untouched. This assumption is particularly limiting when the tool faces domain shift, as segmentation errors can undermine even correct reasoning. We therefore argue that the segmentation tool should be optimized together with the reasoning policy. However, this is challenging because policy optimization and differentiable tool learning rely on fundamentally different objectives. In this work, we introduce group relative tool optimization (GRTO), a mathematically grounded two-stage framework for jointly optimizing a policy and its differentiable tool. The key idea is to first align the tool with the policy expected after joint training, rather than the initial policy. The prealigned tool then leads to a more robust reward signal and superior policy convergence in subsequent policy training. In the first stage, GRTO bootstraps the tool toward the theoretically optimal policy, capturing readily attainable gains without costly on-policy rollouts. This alignment bootstraps the second stage, where GRTO extends GRPO to jointly refine the policy and tool. Across three challenging referring segmentation benchmarks, GRTO achieves substantial improvements over plain GRPO and alternative tool training procedures, matching or surpassing domain-specific state-of-the-art methods. This demonstrates the value of unifying reinforcement learning with differentiable auxiliary objectives for reasoning-intensive segmentation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SEE: Unlocking the Hidden Perception of Frozen VLMs
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) grasp the overall content of an image but often miss the fine details a question hinges on, such as a small object in a large photo or a number in a dense infographic. Yet even when their answer is wrong, the region they point to often contains the evidence. We introduce Self-Elicited Evidence (SEE), a training-free method that lets a frozen VLM look again where it points. When the initial answer has low confidence, SEE prompts the model to propose regions where the details may appear, answers the question on these enlarged crops, and aggregates the answers with the original prediction through confidence-weighted voting. The model also answers with its own transcript, which helps on text-rich images. SEE needs no detector or OCR engine. Across five backbones, SEE improves every small-object benchmark by 2.3-13.1 points and outperforms five training-free baselines on small objects. With SEE, Qwen3.5-4B surpasses the direct answer of Qwen3.5-9B and matches the 6 times larger Qwen3.5-27B.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: DORMS: Image Segmentation via Depth-Ordered Region Merge Trees
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We introduce DORMS (Depth-Ordered Region Merging for Segmentation), a purely algorithmic approach to image segmentation from monocular depth maps, requiring no neural networks or learned parameters in the segmentation process. An off-the-shelf monocular depth estimator provides the input depth maps. Our method constructs depth-ordered merge trees through a deterministic union-find sweep, combining component area, depth persistence, and spatial contact constraints to guide region merging. A threshold search determines the segmentation granularity according to a specified target region count, while global depth detrending improves the separation of local geometric structures. Extensive experiments on COCO Panoptic, Cityscapes, and ADE20K demonstrate consistent improvements over classical segmentation baselines and competitive performance against zero-shot neural segmentation models. Notably, our method outperforms all evaluated zero-shot models on Cityscapes, while remaining competitive with several approaches on COCO and ADE20K. These results highlight the potential of purely algorithmic geometric reasoning for image segmentation without learned segmentation models.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 18 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Project page: https://heaveho-humanoid.github.io/

Cryptography and Security.title: Is Randomness Necessary for Adaptive Data Analysis?
Cryptography and Security.summary:
The Adaptive Data Analysis (ADA) problem formalizes the challenge of preventing false discovery and overfitting when a dataset is repeatedly reused. Formally, our input is a dataset containing $n$ i.i.d. samples from an unknown distribution $\mathcal{P}$ over a domain $\mathcal{X}$, and our goal is to answer a sequence of $k$ adaptively chosen statistical queries with respect to $\mathcal{P}$. The main question is how many queries we can support (i.e., how large $k$ can be), primarily as a function of the number of samples $n$. This question has been intensively studied and is relatively well-understood for randomized mechanisms: there are computationally efficient mechanisms that support $k \approx n^2$ queries, and no computationally efficient mechanism can answer $k \gg n^2$ queries. In this paper, we address a fundamental question: is randomness necessary for ADA?
  Despite a decade of work on ADA, this question remains open. A folklore observation dating back to the initial works on ADA is that randomness is {\em not} necessary when the analyst is computationally bounded. Yet, the necessity of randomness against computationally unbounded analysts has remained elusive. Our main contribution resolves this gap in the information-theoretic setting. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that randomness is {\em strictly necessary} to answer a non-trivial number of adaptive queries: when the analyst is unbounded, any deterministic mechanism can be forced to fail after just $k = \tilde{O}(n)$ queries.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Contains a new proof in the plain model, using domain of size 2^{poly(n)}

Cryptography and Security.title: "I Don't Think It's a Scam": A First Look at Family Intervention Barriers in Elder Abuse Discussions on Reddit and Baidu Tieba
Cryptography and Security.summary: When older adults trust scammers despite warnings, families face obstacles to intervention. Complainants aged 60 and older reported \$4.9 billion in losses in 2024 to the U.S. Internet Crime Complaint Center. To investigate family intervention barriers to elder scams, we collected 2M Reddit posts from May 2021 to June 2026 and 2B Baidu Tieba posts from 2007 to 2026. The final corpora contain 13,082 Reddit posts and 3,933 Baidu Tieba posts, labeled using platform-specific codebooks, manual reference annotations, and LLM coding. Through a mixed-methods analysis, we find that scams often extend beyond a single incident and are reported alongside debt problems and broken family relationships. In 68.0\% of Reddit posts recording reactions, older adults showed resistance or continued involvement; in Baidu Tieba family-confrontation posts, 41.9\% showed continued belief. Relatives identified fraud in 74.4\% of Reddit posts and narrated cases on Baidu Tieba, but without the victim's consent, relatives may lack the legal authority to intervene. In Reddit posts recording reactions, account locks or credential changes appeared in 8.9\% under resistance or continued involvement, compared with 33.3\% under acceptance. Measures such as phone or network monitoring and financial takeover were reported more often under resistance. Recovering funds is very limited in posts recording follow-up results of fraud; Baidu Tieba users reported that police classified older adults' voluntary transfers as civil disputes.

Cryptography and Security.title: LLM-Guided Cyber-Physical Attack Path Identification in Smart Grids
Cryptography and Security.summary: Identifying high-impact attack paths in cyber-physical power systems is critical for improving grid resilience. Existing methods typically rely on either structural topology analysis or simulation-based cascading-failure models. Topology-based approaches capture connectivity but lack adversarial reasoning, while simulation-driven methods are primarily suited for offline analysis and are less effective for rapid evaluation of evolving attack scenarios. As a result, identifying realistic attack paths that jointly capture topology, threat semantics, and physical impact remains challenging. This paper presents a physics-grounded framework for identifying cyber-physical attack paths using large language models (LLMs), with cascading-failure-derived impact rankings used as physics-grounded references. The framework integrates system topology, LLM-guided STRIDE and MITRE ATT&CK threat modeling, and three baseline strategies for comparison: topology-driven, threat-driven, and fusion-based. Evaluation is performed using (i) critical-node overlap between LLM-inferred top-K rankings and cascading-failure-based ground truth; (ii) node-level similarity between LLM-inferred and reference paths; and (iii) path-level alignment capturing agreement in complete attack sequences. Results show that structured LLM-based threat modeling substantially improves alignment with physics-grounded references. In the cyber layer, critical-node overlap@3 increases from approximately 33% to as high as 100%, while node-level similarity reaches up to 65% and path-level alignment reaches up to 48%. In addition, the proposed framework reduces runtime by approximately 75--85% compared to the fusion-based baseline in the IEEE 14-bus system. These results suggest that LLM-guided attack path identification is a promising approach for efficient and impact-aware cyber-physical security analysis.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Accepted at IEEE IECON 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Threshold Choice, Not Sample Size, Bounds Trustless Verification of Nondeterministic Compound AI Workflows
Cryptography and Security.summary: Compound AI pipelines chain LLM calls, retrievers, and tools and are nondeterministic: sampling, model updates, and volatile tool responses make one input yield different outputs across runs. Such pipelines increasingly run across edge, cloud, and orbital nodes owned by no single party, whose optimizations discard intermediate results before inspection. Verifying reproduction there means tolerating nondeterministic outputs, a node that may not report honestly, and intermittent access to any shared record; existing work addresses at most two at once. We give a protocol covering all three: it commits digests of each stage's inputs, outputs, and context under a policy digest pinning the metric and threshold, anchors them without trusting the executing node, defers under partition, and decides a challenge on the median of $k$ re-executions, with no quorum. Where that procedure breaks is the main result. On a synthetic HotpotQA pipeline a calibrated fixed threshold accepts 44 of 45 honest reproductions and rejects 104 of 105 divergent pairs, yet lets same-input fabrication through in 27 of 29 trials at k=5, more samples being no help since sampling sharpens an estimate without moving it. Holding that metric and this pipeline's re-execution spread fixed, the binding constraint is the threshold rather than the sample size: one derived per execution detects 19 of 29 where the best constant matched to the same zero honest rejections reaches 9, rejects no honest commitment at k=5 though 3 of 15 at k=3, and catches 11 of 15 of an attacker built against it, which has to aim at a target drawn only after its commitment exists. That rule is measured rather than deployed.

Cryptography and Security.title: Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Language Models via Infilling
Cryptography and Security.summary: Memorization in large language models has been studied almost exclusively through prefix-conditioned extraction, a natural choice for autoregressive models. However, diffusion language models (DLMs) can denoise masked tokens at arbitrary positions. Thus, prefix-only probing reveals only one facet of memorization in DLMs and significantly underestimates the risk of training-data extraction. In order to realistically model extractability of training data in DLMs, we introduce infilling extraction, a data-extraction protocol parameterized by an arbitrary binary mask that subsumes prefix-only probing and accounts for the bidirectional inductive bias of DLMs. Instantiating it on LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B across five extraction modes, three training pipelines, and three corpora covering verbatim and partial leakage, we find that mask geometry governs extractability: edge-conditioned masks extract up to three times more verbatim sequences than prefix-conditioned ones, and bidirectional access opens channels inaccessible in autoregressive models. In particular, an adversary who obtains a PII-redacted copy of the training data can use targeted infilling to raise PII recall on fine-tuned DLMs by 2.5-4.5x over prefix-conditioned extraction, substantially narrowing the gap to a scale-matched autoregressive model and, for LLaDA on email addresses, exceeding it under greedy prefix-conditioned extraction. Tunable parameters for decoding measurably affect extraction performance, while a follow-up supervised fine-tuning stage does not eliminate the prior memorization.
Cryptography and Security.comment: NeurIPS 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Stealing Exact Training Data from Other Clients during Federated Learning
Cryptography and Security.summary: Malicious adversaries can employ gradient inversion attacks to reverse-engineer private data using the model updates of a round in Federated Learning. While there have been developments in gradient inversion for text, exact text recovery by a malicious client has so far remained infeasible, as FedAvg entangles the gradient contributions of many clients and obscures the signal of any individual sentence. We introduce a novel attack pipeline that unwinds this entanglement progressively through an iterative loop, in which the gradient contributions of sentences recovered exactly in one round are subtracted from the aggregate, exposing the remaining sentences for recovery in the next iteration. We show, for the first time, exact sentence recovery, with 100% precision, and on aggregates containing up to $4\times$ more tokens than the model's hidden dimension, we recover up to 80.2% of client sentences exactly, a regime where existing attacks recover none exactly.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Preprint. 22 pages, 21 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: The Limit Is in the Input, Not the Model: State-Dependent Command Safety in Natural-Language Interfaces to Industrial Controllers
Cryptography and Security.summary: Language models judging commands to industrial controllers may not receive machine state, the equipment's current condition. The same command can require opposite safety decisions in different states, so an incorrect answer may reflect missing information rather than poor reasoning. We propose an answerability audit: does the model receive the information needed to decide? The audit records the model's inputs and pairs the same command with two states requiring opposite answers. The paired score counts a pair only when both answers are correct. We add rules, then state values, to the model's input. In an author-built test of 15 pairs from three systems with four language models, none reliably distinguished the paired cases without state, even with rules. With state, scores ranged from 0 to 13 correct pairs out of 15; three models improved. With text alone, one model always allowed commands and another always denied them. Their overall (raw) accuracies differed by 32 percentage points; both scored 50% balanced accuracy, which weights safe and unsafe cases equally, and no correct pairs. A rule evaluator matched all 15 pairs by applying the same rules that supplied the expected answers; this is not an independent safety test. The audit complements systems that check actions against safety rules: it checks whether the model receives the information needed for those decisions. This helps evaluators separate missing-input problems from model errors. These small-sample scores do not establish general model reliability.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 8 pages. Accepted for publication in the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining Workshops (ICDMW), 6th Machine Learning for Cybersecurity (MLC) Workshop

Cryptography and Security.title: Analysis of Commit Signing on GitHub
Cryptography and Security.summary: Since 1999, the security community has known that managing cryptographic keys is hard for users of cryptographic systems. Git lets software developers use private keys they control to digitally sign the commits that record their code changes to a repository. This practice offers a rare opportunity to study how a large community manages cryptographic keys in everyday work. In this paper, we study end-to-end commit signing, using GitHub accounts as our sampling unit. Our 2% stratified sample of the GitHub population comprises 2,737,649 accounts, 71,694 of which have made at least one commit. For these accounts, we analyze 16,112,439 commits across 874,198 repositories and collect 208,546 public keys uploaded to the sampled accounts. We examine developers' signing key usage patterns and compare our findings with those of prior commit signing studies, most of which used repository-based samples and paid less attention to key management. We then outline a path toward more usable key management for developers.

Cryptography and Security.title: Gradient-Based Defensive Poisoning Against System Identification Attacks on Cyber-Physical Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary: AI-driven attacks learn the models of cyber-physical systems (CPS) by passively observing controller and plant signals, then use this knowledge to act covertly. Because covertness depends on the accuracy of the identified model, degrading that accuracy is a viable countermeasure. This work applies Adversarial Machine Learning as a defense, injecting small perturbations into the measurements the attacker observes to degrade an artificial neural network (ANN)-based system identification (SI) attack. The perturbations are derived from input gradients of several independently trained identification models, aggregated into a generalized perturbation, and confined to the transient regimes that carry most of the dynamic information. A sparsity parameter further restricts them to the most influential samples, with negligible cost in effectiveness. On a simulated DC motor networked control system, the proposed perturbations induce larger prediction errors than stochastic poisoning of equal root-mean-square magnitude, and the advantage widens as the magnitude grows. This limits the defense's operating range, which is intended for decoy environments such as CPS honeynets. Additional results indicate that the designed poisoning signals can also degrade N4SID-based system identification, providing evidence of their transferability beyond the ANN-based models originally targeted.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Presented at the 2026 IEEE International Workshop on Technologies for Defense and Security (TechDefense 2026), Torino, Italy, November 4-6, 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: ChainIT Transaction Truth: Stablecoins, Web3 Wallets, and Multi-Rail Commerce. A Zero-Trust Control Plane for Verified Identity, Organizational Authority, Runtime Compliance, Secure Wallet Execution, and Immutable Settlement Evidence
Cryptography and Security.summary: Stablecoins can move value continuously across programmable networks, and Web3 wallets can authorize those transfers with cryptographic signatures, but neither capability, standing alone, establishes a complete commercial transaction. A blockchain may prove that a transaction satisfied protocol rules, and a wallet may prove that sufficient signing authority existed; neither proves who initiated the transaction, for which legal entity, under what current authority, against which current compliance evidence, on what exact instruction, or with what settlement and accounting outcome. We describe the ChainIT Transaction Truth Architecture, a zero-trust control, execution, and evidence architecture that places verified individual and organizational identity, the organizational authority record and authority policy of the ChainIT Authority Protocol, transaction-specific runtime compliance decisions, exact-digest approval, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use Execution Authorization Credential in front of wallet execution, and that records settlement, reconciliation, and lifecycle evidence after the transaction. The architecture separates five boundaries: control of a key is not identity, identity is not organizational authority, authority is not compliance, compliance is not execution authority, and network confirmation is not complete commercial settlement. We describe wallet and custody profiles, including a multi-party computation (MPC) profile in which custody security is kept independent of business authority, stablecoin and Web3 evidence domains, layered finality, the U.S. stablecoin regulatory context as of September 2026, and a phased deployment in which pilot success requires that the control invariants hold under attack and failure.
Cryptography and Security.comment: ChainIT white paper CIT-TT-EWP-2.1. 29 pages, 4 figures. Companion papers: Provable Authority (arXiv:2610.22899), Provable Compliance (arXiv:2610.22913). Project page: https://chainit.com/white-papers/

Cryptography and Security.title: Robust, Lightweight Locally Differentially Private Histogram Estimation and the Role of Dropout Attacks
Cryptography and Security.summary: Local differential privacy (LDP) is vulnerable to output manipulation by malicious clients. Zero-knowledge proofs can enforce correct report computation, but clients may still selectively drop out after inspecting their outputs. Prior work combines zero-knowledge proofs with homomorphic encryption to hide reports from clients and prevent selective dropout, but incurs substantial computational cost. We instead develop a three-message lightweight verification framework for robust histogram estimation that uses proofs of plaintext evaluation to restrict output manipulation to selective dropout. Across the evaluated settings for PI-RAPPOR and Hadamard Response, mean per-client online latency remains below 500 milliseconds. We further establish tight error bounds showing that, for RAPPOR, PI-RAPPOR, and Hadamard Response, restricting malicious clients to selective dropout reduces attack-dependent error by a factor proportional to the square root of the domain size compared with output manipulation. Additionally, when client protocols cannot be modified, we propose server-side consistency checks for RAPPOR and Hadamard Response. These checks improve robustness without client-side cryptography and can be applied post-hoc to collected reports, offering an alternative under different deployment constraints. Experiments demonstrate that both verification and consistency checks substantially reduce attack error for certain mechanisms, with consistency checks yielding errors intermediate between those obtained with verification and those under unrestricted output manipulation.

Cryptography and Security.title: TROPT: An Open Framework for Unifying and Advancing Discrete Text Optimization
Cryptography and Security.summary: Discrete text-trigger optimization -- searching for text sequences that, when ingested by a model, steer it toward a specified objective -- underpins model red-teaming (e.g., LLM jailbreaks), as well as auditing and interpretability. However, the current state of discrete optimizers hinders their adoption and progress. First, existing optimizers, when open-sourced at all, are scattered across research codebases tied to specific models, objectives, and problem domains. Second, optimizers proliferate, each requiring engineering overhead to use or extend, and remaining hard to compare head-to-head. Together, these raise the bar for adopting optimizers in existing or new domains, and for advancing them via new strategies. We address these gaps with TROPT, the first open-source framework that unifies discrete optimizers' execution and standardizes their development under a single interface. TROPT makes it easy to customize end-to-end optimization recipes by swapping any component -- models, objectives, and optimizers -- extending its reach across domains and new applications. TROPT currently ships with 40+ optimization recipes -- covering applications such as jailbreaking and probing model internals -- built from 15+ optimizers (spanning white-box to black-box access) and 15+ losses, from foundational to state-of-the-art methods. Demonstrating its utility, we leverage TROPT in several studies: (i) controlled, large-scale experiments comparing and enhancing optimization strategies for LLM jailbreaks, revealing potent-yet-underadopted techniques; and (ii) porting optimizers across applications and domains (e.g., from LLM jailbreaks to corpus poisoning). In all, TROPT significantly lowers the barrier to adopting and advancing discrete text optimization.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations & Datasets Track)

Cryptography and Security.title: Playing the SMR Game with Existential Honesty
Cryptography and Security.summary:
State machine replication protocols are usually proven secure in the honest-Byzantine setting, which requires an honest supermajority of validators. Deployed systems offer no such guarantee: validators participate for profit and may deviate from the protocol whenever doing so increases their gains. In our work, every validator is rational or Byzantine, and none is honest. Rational validators may collude with each other and with the Byzantine ones, who may also bribe them to deviate. Known impossibility results show that, without honest validators, clients that decide whether to accept a transaction based on a non-interactive certificate and without further communication cannot be kept safe. To bypass these results, we let clients relay the certificates they receive to full nodes and wait before confirming transactions. We also assume that one full node, whose identity is unknown, is honest and always online.
  Under this assumption, we build a finalization layer over any certifiable quorum-based protocol in a synchronous network. Clients run an existing freezing gadget and fetch past certificates from the honest full node, which makes the protocol \emph{always-safe}: no two honest clients confirm conflicting ledgers, for any strategy of the validators. We incentivize participation through rewards, which the adversary may use to bribe rational validators into censoring transactions. In this setting, we formalize censorship and characterize it tightly: paying only with his rewards, the adversary censors less than a $\bw$ fraction of the available fees at each height, where $\bw$ is the fraction of the quorum he signs, and every coin of censorship beyond that comes from his own funds.

Cryptography and Security.title: Adversarial Process Disturbances at a Deployable Alarm Budget: Detector Evaluation on a Simulator and a Real Plant
Cryptography and Security.summary: Industrial anomaly detection is evaluated largely on simulators, and recent work reports large drops, with unstable rankings, on real plant data. We ask whether that extends to the security case. We evaluate eleven detectors across classical, neural, dependency and causal families on a simulated chemical process and a sodium thermal-hydraulic facility: different processes sharing no equipment, but both continuous, at steady state, and perturbed only through temperature, pressure, flow and valve, never composition. Three conditions prior work does not cover: disturbances authored against a threat model rather than native faults; one construction applied to both processes; and detection read at a declared false-alarm budget. The drop persists throughout. The simulator panel looks deployable, neural matching classical; on plant telemetry detection collapses and the neural family trails, a gap that in-sample thresholds likely understate. Which detector wins transfers between the two processes; how often it fires does not. Two results hold on both. Sequential valve manipulation defeats the whole panel: at tier 2 no detector flags more than 0.17 of its perturbed samples, against 0.89 or better for most disturbances. And the plant's collapse is not merely that its disturbances are weaker, though they are by about twelvefold; matched on measured strength, the plant is never the better detected.
Cryptography and Security.comment: v2: results regenerated after defect fixes. Two defective disturbance generators removed (now nine disturbances on the plant, seven on the simulator). Autoencoder rerun after an attack-labelling fix. Cross-process rank comparison now uses the per-disturbance aggregation stated in the method; ranking correlation reported as a positive association. Cost, regime and alarm-budget claims narrowed

Cryptography and Security.title: SCR: Detecting Backdoor-Poisoned Samples through Clean-Reference Residuals
Cryptography and Security.summary: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which adversaries manipulate model predictions by injecting poisoned samples into training data. Detecting these samples remains challenging because legitimate semantic variation can obscure poisoning-related signals in learned representations. Consequently, class-level statistics used by existing detectors may flag benign feature deviations while overlooking poisoned samples that blend into the class distribution. In this paper, we propose Semantic Counterfactual Residualization (SCR), which uses a small set of clean reference samples to account for benign variation through sample-specific feature reconstruction. SCR identifies poisoned samples by detecting coherent deviations from these clean baselines, without requiring prior knowledge of the attacks. We evaluate SCR through experiments covering twelve dirty-label and clean-label attacks across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet. With a small clean-reference set, SCR achieves attack-averaged true positive rates above 99.5\% and false positive rates below 2\% on each dataset, outperforming eight representative detection baselines in macro-TPR.

Cryptography and Security.title: Language Model Security Modules: Turning LLM Interpretability into Runtime Defense
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are served behind layered defenses such as alignment and guardrail models, yet jailbreaks still get through. Interpretability research looks inside the model, where methods such as probes and sparse autoencoders expose signals of harmful content during generation. A signal alone, however, is not a defense. To become one, the serving system must tie each signal to the right request, apply the policy as declared, and release output only when the policy allows. Today, defenses built on such signals handle these duties on their own, so every new detector needs its own integration. Yet none of these duties depends on how a signal is computed. We present Language Model Security Modules (LMSM), which adapts the design of Linux Security Modules to LLM serving and carries out these duties once in a shared mediation path. The path hosts pluggable backends that turn model internals into evidence and policies that decide what that evidence allows. Each policy declares the evidence and evaluations it needs, and LMSM provides exactly these for each request and verifies that they took place, so a failure is never mistaken for permission. Protection therefore remains cheap and correct under common serving optimizations. We evaluate LMSM in vLLM, with both eager and compiled execution, on Qwen3-4B and Gemma-3-4B with fitted probes, a released transcoder, and a released sparse autoencoder. With vLLM's default optimizations on, every backend keeps at least 96% of native throughput, and all of them share the same mediation path. On Qwen3-4B, a representative probe-based policy cuts HarmBench attack success from 39.4% to 3.3% while XSTest false refusals rise from 0.8% to 3.1%. LMSM lets existing and future interpretability methods become runtime defenses without rebuilding the serving path.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 17 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Code: https://github.com/xiuyuz/LMSM

Cryptography and Security.title: obfsgen: Generative Tunnel Obfuscation
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Encrypted tunnels are widely used to circumvent censorship, which has drawn censors' efforts to detect and block them. As the circumvention tunnels in widest use have largely converged on TLS, detection has shifted from the content of their traffic to its shape, where recent research and real-world blocking events have revealed exploitable fingerprints of tunneling. Existing traffic-shaping obfuscators such as obfs4, however, are fundamentally limited in hiding these fingerprints, as their application-driven design can only add to the shape that the application creates. A schedule-driven obfuscator, which decides when and how much to send independently of the application, can give tunnels any shape but raises new challenges, first and foremost what a good shape is.
  This paper presents obfsgen, a schedule-driven obfuscator for tunneling traffic. obfsgen samples its schedule from a generative sequence model of normal traffic, which predicts the future shape of a flow from its whole history, to capture the long-range dependencies that make a flow's shape normal. Built around this model, obfsgen addresses system problems that such an obfuscator faces in practice, such as synchronization across a noisy network. We evaluate the (in)distinguishability that obfsgen offers, the performance overhead that it adds and the computational resources that it requires. We see the schedule-driven architecture as the next generation of tunnel obfuscators, and we hope that obfsgen and the rationale behind its design help make such obfuscators practical and deployable.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Preprint, 20 pages, 14 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: RECLAIM: Robot-Vision-Informed Adversarial Patch Defense via Embodied Attention Feedback
Cryptography and Security.summary: Vision-language-action policies control embodied agents through a perception-action loop grounded in physical interaction, where adversarial patches can corrupt action predictions and thereby alter subsequent observations. To mitigate these threats, many existing defenses rely on policy adaptation or auxiliary models, but require additional training or inference. We introduce RECLAIM, a training-free, inference-time defense that uses a frozen VLA's own attention response to local visual interventions to guide purification during closed-loop embodied manipulation. Our key insight is that attention changes induced by local edits provide feedback for choosing where and how to purify as the robot interacts with its environment. RECLAIM combines this feedback with robot geometry to refine patch localization and select local treatments, then revalidates them as the agent's embodied actions change the observed scene. We evaluate RECLAIM against patches generated by four adversarial attack methods across multiple manipulation task suites under frozen VLA control. Under adversarial patch attacks, RECLAIM succeeds in at least one rollout on 95% of the evaluated tasks and raises rollout success on LIBERO-Object from 0% without defense to 70.0%. Its mean decision time is only 548.9 ms per control step. These results highlight policy-guided visual purification as an effective approach to defending embodied agents against adversarial patches and recovering closed-loop task execution.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 10 pages, 2 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: Probing agent overeagerness in realistic settings with continuation audits
Cryptography and Security.summary: Frontier coding agents increasingly exhibit overeagerness, taking surprising, sometimes reckless actions beyond a user's mandate --- reported in recent system cards from frontier model developers. These cases are surfaced through internal deployment monitoring, which requires private traffic and is out of reach for open-weight models and independent evaluators. Automated alignment audits are the natural alternative, but capable models increasingly recognise the synthetic setup and adjust their behaviour. We introduce Continuation Audits, a pipeline that grounds the auditor on a prefix drawn from a real coding-agent transcript and directs it to continue the trajectory toward a seeded behaviour. Because the prefix is drawn from a real session, the auditor only needs to maintain a realistic setting rather than manufacturing it. We validate the method on SWE-Chat prefixes: on a paired subset of 90 audits a judge cannot reliably distinguish continuations from their source sessions (realism win rate 0.42 vs.\ 0.43), and across all 900 audits verbalized eval-awareness does not exceed the rate observed in the unaudited real sessions. Applying the pipeline to three recent models across three seeds, we find each model leads a different seed --- DeepSeek~V4~Pro on colleague-credentials misuse, GPT-5.6~Terra on file-permission bypasses, and Kimi~K3 on treating diagnostic questions as instructions. Kimi~K3 additionally continues to bypass file-permission protections after an explicit CLAUDE.md prohibition while the other two stop entirely, corroborating Moonshot's own report of excessive proactiveness.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Presented at NeurIPS Workshops: (1) Third Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond, and (2) The 1st Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB) at NeurIPS 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Mitigating fix reversal: Counterfactual constraints for function-level vulnerability detection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Function-level vulnerability detectors often exhibit fix reversal, assigning a higher vulnerability probability to a fixed version than to its vulnerable counterpart. Fixes usually lengthen functions, and larger length increases are associated with more severe reversal. Code-transformation experiments indicate that fix reversal mainly stems from a length shortcut: vulnerability probability increases with function length when content is fixed. We propose CFVul to address this problem. Sliding-window encoding covers complete functions, retaining fix information beyond the truncation boundary. During training, a content constraint encourages the vulnerable version to receive a higher vulnerability probability under a common length input. During inference, a length constraint averages vulnerability probabilities over fixed reference lengths, reducing the influence of actual length changes. On PrimeVul, CFVul achieves a fix-pair ranking metric, PairRank, of 59.4\%, exceeding the existing methods compared. For fixes that increase function length by more than 15\%, PairRank rises from CodeBERT's 25.8\% to 48.4\%. PairRank also improves in experiments with four additional models and three additional datasets. By weakening the length shortcut, CFVul reduces cases in which fixed versions receive higher vulnerability probabilities than vulnerable versions. It requires only existing fix pairs and applies to multiple pretrained code models, facilitating adoption in existing detectors.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 21 pages, 9 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: Drift-Aware Explainable Prioritization for Windows PE Malware Forensic Triage with Semantic Consistency Checks
Cryptography and Security.summary: Forensic investigators must decide which suspicious files to examine first. Machine-learning (ML) and deep-learning (DL) malware detectors usually return a bare score that neither explains why a file deserves attention nor signals when changing data make the model unreliable. We present a framework for Windows Portable Executable (PE) malware forensic triage that works only on pre-extracted static features and never executes malware. A calibrated maliciousness score sets each file's triage priority, and a per-sample feature attribution explains the prediction. A per-sample consistency score measures whether the top attributed features agree with documented behaviors from the Malware Behavior Catalog (MBC) and MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques & Common Knowledge (ATT&CK), where the available features support such interpretation. Conformal evaluation and statistical distribution tests flag drift. Each file receives one investigator-oriented triage output. The evaluation protocol, specified before testing, uses a time-ordered split of EMBER2024 as the primary dataset and BODMAS for family disjoint checks, and compares every component with simple baselines on predictive performance, prioritization effectiveness, explanation quality and robustness over time.

Cryptography and Security.title: PoCoFL: A Framework for POlicy-COmpliant Federated Learning
Cryptography and Security.summary: Federated Learning (FL) is a privacy-oriented learning paradigm that enables collaborative model training while keeping training data local to clients. However, FL does not guarantee that clients submit policy-compliant contributions or that aggregators process admitted contributions correctly. Update-magnitude bounds alone cannot ensure compliance with learning-specific requirements involving private data, intermediate models, or retained state. These requirements differ across FL settings, motivating a unified framework to specify and verify client and aggregation policies. This work introduces PoCoFL, a policy-compliant federated learning framework that separates three aspects: (i) FL type, (ii) policy semantics, and (iii) cryptographic realisation. We provide a formalisation that captures client and aggregation requirements as policy-dependent relations, defining update admissibility, aggregation correctness, and policy-relative privacy. These relations enable verification of selected properties of intermediate objects, such as local-model loss, continual-learning state, and personalised optimisation conditions, in each round. Clients demonstrate compliance of their contributions using compatible cryptographic mechanisms, while aggregators prove that the recorded set of admitted contributions was processed according to the selected aggregation policy. We demonstrate PoCoFL through four formal instantiations and corresponding proof-of-concept realisations: (i) vanilla, (ii) continual, (iii) personalised, and (iv) threshold-encrypted federated learning. We evaluate how policy enforcement affects the learning objectives of vanilla, personalised, and continual FL, and quantify the computational and communication overhead of policy verification across all four instantiations. These results demonstrate that PoCoFL captures complex policy representations across the evaluated FL settings.

Cryptography and Security.title: Who Is Behind the Harness? Verifying Model Identity in Coding Agents through Behavioral Fingerprinting
Cryptography and Security.summary:
LLMs increasingly operate through coding-agent harnesses that inspect repositories, invoke tools, and modify files. Substituting the model behind such an agent can therefore change security-relevant decisions, including whether it verifies changes or recovers safely from failures. Existing LLM fingerprints largely infer identity from direct text or token distributions. In coding agents, these signals are mediated by system instructions, controller logic, tools, and execution feedback, limiting their transfer.
  We present LIDAR (LLM Identification from Decisions and Actions at Runtime), an active black-box fingerprinting method for coding-agent execution. Three coding probe pairs expose post-edit verification, transient-failure recovery, and specification--test conflict resolution under controlled changes. LIDAR represents the resulting trajectories with complementary instance-level and distribution-level features and compares them with clean references using a lightweight probabilistic identifier. It requires no access to model weights, logits, or provider internals.
  We evaluate 24 models from eight families on OpenCode, OpenHands, and mini-swe-agent, fitting separate references for each harness. Closed-set Top-1 accuracy ranges from 91.39\% to 98.89\% across the three harnesses, exceeding all three baselines in each setting. When the audit also includes unregistered models from the same families, balanced accuracy ranges from 79.58\% to 80.42\%. These results show that agent execution behavior provides model-identity evidence beyond final outputs.

Cryptography and Security.title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 18 pages, 6 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: Hearsay: Who Can Audit the Record a Deployed Agent Harness Writes?
Cryptography and Security.summary: The record of an agent's run is written by the harness that drives the agent. When the run is later disputed, the auditor was not there and has only this record. We ask whether someone who was not there can check the record, and what decides the answer. It depends on who wrote what a check can rely on: if the harness wrote all of it, the record is only the harness's own word, and we call it hearsay. We build Hearsay, a benchmark that examines the record and not the task: five harnesses run fourteen tasks, model examiners from three vendors and a human panel read the records and answer questions about the runs, and every passage they cite is labelled mechanically by who wrote it. We also audit what is deployed: in all sixteen frameworks, the harness is the only writer. With one writer, readers can name the fault from the record, in up to nine runs in ten, but they cannot check the record. The model examiners claim corroboration for 18 to 55 points more of their evidence than the labels support, a gap we then predicted for runs driven by another vendor's model and found again. And the best of them notices only half of the alterations we make to a record, while the two that name the fault most often cannot tell what a harness left out. With a second writer, the record can be checked. Our sandbox keeps a ledger of what passes between harness and model, and reading the ledger against the record in both directions shows what the record leaves out and what it adds. We test this as an auditor would use it, on one unseen record at a time. On runs driven by a third vendor's model, with every rule committed before the records existed, it reports 64 of 66 alterations and flags none of 84 clean records. On held-out records in five formats it reports 109 of 115. What makes a record evidence is a second writer, not a better reader.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 50 pages (10-page main text), 8 figures. Under review. v2: re-organized around one question; the second writer is now evaluated one unseen record at a time, on held-out records and under rules committed before the records existed; title changed. Code and data: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/hearsay-4E7C

Cryptography and Security.title: AutoPI: Taxonomy-Guided Adaptive Red Teaming for Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: Prompt injection is the dominant unsolved security risk for LLM agents, and the community now agrees that robustness must be measured against adaptive attackers rather than fixed benchmark injections. Many adaptive red teamers exist, and most are built to maximize attack success rate (ASR). Yet ASR counts how often a target breaks, not in how many different ways. A red teamer can achieve a high ASR by reusing a few techniques that work, leaving the others untested and absent from the attacks used to harden models. We present AutoPI, an adaptive red teamer designed to find many different ways to break a target, not just to break it often. AutoPI uses PIAtlas, a taxonomy of prompt-injection techniques, both to guide its search and to measure coverage. For each scenario, an attacker LLM writes an injection for every sub-technique in the taxonomy and then reworks the ones that fail using feedback from an LLM judge. The method is black-box and training-free, it plugs into existing benchmarks in place of their fixed attack templates, and it stays up to date as the taxonomy evolves. We evaluate AutoPI on AgentDojo and IPI Arena against open-weight and proprietary target models. Alongside ASR, we report technique coverage, the fraction of taxonomy classes, techniques, and sub-techniques that yield at least one successful injection. On AgentDojo, AutoPI finds a successful injection against Qwen3.6-35B in all six classes of the taxonomy and for more than 90% of its techniques. Against Claude Haiku 5.5, the most robust target we evaluate, it achieves between 20% and 50% higher ASR and between 25% and 400% higher class-level coverage than recent state-of-the-art adaptive red teamers, while requiring no training. We release our code and the generated attacks to support reproducible, coverage-aware evaluation.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 18 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables. Project page at https://stevendamianakis.github.io/autopi-site/ and code at https://github.com/stevendamianakis/autopi

Cryptography and Security.title: When Shuffling Fails: Token Recovery from Obfuscated KV Caches
Cryptography and Security.summary:
LLM serving systems store, offload, and share KV caches, exposing token-level representations to infrastructure operators and co-tenants. Shuffled obfuscation combines secret linear transforms with fresh permutations, claiming security from b! possible shufflings. We show that input symmetry invalidates this counting argument: security depends on distinguishable outputs under chosen inputs. Repeated tokens produce identical first-layer Value rows, making every row permutation leave the data unchanged. Only auxiliary structures such as a single-row recovery marker vary, reducing the effective state space from b! to b.
  We construct Repeat-to-Reveal. The attacker collects the b distinguishable states from its own probes and exploits their rank-one differences to recover an equivalent denoiser without knowing the defender's secret parameters. A one-time calibration transfers across requests sharing the same secret epoch, enabling passive token-multiset recovery from subsequently observed cache blocks through public-model dictionary matching. We instantiate the attack on official KV-Cloak and evaluate 3,000 real WildChat user prompts across nine models and eleven configurations. The attack recovers the secret parameters with high accuracy and achieves 100 percent token-multiset recovery on GPU. Refreshing row-level secrets between epochs interrupts cross-request transfer, confirming secret reuse scope as the operative vulnerability. We further confirm orbit collapse on two other open-source defenses: the sequence-permutation implementation of Thomas et al. and PermLLM. The KV-Cloak developers invited a detailed report through their private vulnerability reporting channel.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 18 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: Retained Encrypted Search with Certified Split Joins
Cryptography and Security.summary: Retaining encrypted search across data edits and worker replacement requires separating computational validity from current release authority. We give exact Hamming search with at most one authorized decryption and decoding attempt per query preparation. Under authenticated prescribed execution, exclusive nonrollback owner state, an ideal public seed-expansion interface and a stated observation model, we reduce bounded adaptive privacy to ordinary ring learning with errors (Ring-LWE). Expanded second components depend only on public masks and fixed maps, independently of queries and the fresh database key. This compiler invariant permits a retained split join against a smaller-modulus encrypted database. A simultaneous bound on the completed circuit covers a finite honest reservation family, including adaptive queries and slot selection, with explicit statistical correctness and privacy losses. In three post-calibration local CPU comparisons on 32,768 vectors of 512 bits, the 60-bit-join construction takes a median 9.825 s for an end-to-end two-query workload, versus 12.159 s for the optimized full-source-modulus baseline. These times include setup, transfers, preparation and private completion. They are local implementation results, not deployment or concrete-security claims.

Cryptography and Security.title: PMKPIR: Parallel Multi-Keyword PIR with Interleaved Batching for Private Boolean Retrieval
Cryptography and Security.summary: Keyword Private Information Retrieval (Keyword PIR) allows users to retrieve data associated with specific keywords from a database while protecting query privacy. However, existing Keyword PIR schemes supporting boolean retrieval either incur high computational overhead due to multiple database traversals, or fail to support universal boolean computation. We propose PMKPIR, a novel keyword PIR scheme supporting both parallel multi-keyword queries and universal boolean computation. We utilize the single instruction multiple data (SIMD) capability of BFV homomorphic encryption to propose an interleaved batching method, and design IBPIR based on this method, achieving the private matching of multiple keywords in a single database traversal. Furthermore, we design a boolean query processing method, extending the parallel capability of interleaved batching from keyword querying to boolean query computation, to support universal boolean computation and accelerate boolean operations. Building upon IBPIR, we integrate this method to further design PMKPIR. To the best of our knowledge, PMKPIR is the first Keyword PIR scheme to support multi-keyword batch matching within boolean queries. Security analysis demonstrates that, consistent with existing PIR schemes supporting boolean retrieval, PMKPIR preserves the core security guarantees of classic PIR. Compared with state-of-the-art schemes, PMKPIR reduces query time, communication overhead, storage overhead, and peak memory by up to 79.06%, 75.00%, 97.92%, and 80.26%, respectively.

Cryptography and Security.title: What Survives the Shift from Text to Pixels? Conditional Protection against Prompt Injection in Image-Rendered Documents
Cryptography and Security.summary: Multimodal language models increasingly answer questions over external documents, exposing them to indirect prompt injection: commands planted in untrusted content to hijack the response. Rendering untrusted content as page images lowers attack success on average, leaving open which injected operations survive rendering, at what utility cost, and whether failed image attacks reflect unread commands or commands read but not followed. We pair text and page-image versions of 191 English question-answering sources across six models, measuring marker appending, answer formatting, and answer replacement alongside clean Question-Answering utility. Rendering reduces append and format execution for every model, yet Qwen3-VL-8B still executes image-borne replacement at 77.96\%. Protection also depends on target type, rendering settings, wording, and repetition, and a search over eight fixed attack candidates largely closes the image deficit in appending and formatting for Qwen and Gemini, though not for GPT-5-nano. Utility ratios on original questions range from 93.31\% to 101.61\%, but Qwen falls to 61.99\% when answers combine two evidence spans. Illegibility cannot explain all failed attacks: models often transcribe and identify image-borne commands they do not execute, and trusted user authorization raises execution on unchanged pages. Inside Qwen, patching early attack-region states induces all three operations, more weakly in images. Attention blocking suggests why: a text command acts through its own positions, whereas visual encoding spreads an image command and its target across the instruction page. Rendering thus offers conditional protection, motivating evaluations that report security by model, operation, and attack budget alongside utility.

Cryptography and Security.title: Erased but Recoverable: On the Fragility of Concept Erasure Under Fine-Tuning
Cryptography and Security.summary: Existing concept erasure methods for text-to-image diffusion models primarily focus on suppressing target concepts while preserving non-target generation quality. However, in practical applications, open-source diffusion models are often further adapted through DreamBooth, LoRA, or Custom Diffusion. Such adaptations can reshape internal representations, thereby weakening or even reversing the erasure effects achieved by existing methods. We identify erasure persistence as a key yet underexplored dimension of concept erasure and analyze how downstream fine-tuning reshapes internal representations. Our analysis reveals that fine-tuning of the original model does not uniformly modify the model, but preserves certain high-contribution structures, particularly attention heads with stable output subspaces and response magnitudes. We also observe that, after downstream fine-tuning of concept-erased models, these heads' output representations more readily realign with their pretrained counterparts. Motivated by this observation, we propose Stable-Head-Aware Concept Erasure (SHACE), which improves erasure persistence by preserving stable attention structures during concept erasure. SHACE identifies stability-critical attention heads through Attention-Head Stability Profiling and keeps their corresponding parameter blocks unchanged during erasure via Stable-Head Gradient Preservation. Extensive experiments show that SHACE improves resistance to concept recovery across diverse fine-tuning settings while maintaining strong suppression and non-target generation quality.

Cryptography and Security.title: Guarding the Kingdom of Skill-Based Agents in the AI Dynasty of Computation: Control-Flow Integrity for Agent Skills
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Control-flow integrity (CFI) confines a program to a control-flow graph fixed ahead of time. Procedural agent skills move this control flow into prompt text, and a large language model (LLM) agent decides at runtime whether each step runs in its reasoning, a tool call, or a script. The procedure's control skeleton survives, but its enforceability depends on where each step runs. Many violations, such as overwriting a file before validation, use only operations the skill requires, so permission allowlists admit them. A deviating or prompt-injected model can also evade a monitor by regime migration, for example by claiming that a check passed.
  We present SkillCFI, which carries CFI over to skill-based agents. Its compiler confines LLM interpretation to compile time and derives the agent's instructions and an executable contract from one skill. By a formal enforceability criterion, it enforces obligations whose evidence crosses the tool boundary and rejects a skill whose mandatory obligation leaves nothing to check. A deterministic runtime enforcer admits a tool request only on trusted evidence and refuses unmediated channels such as inline scripts, so admitted traces follow the contract whatever the model proposes.
  On eight self-written skills, no compiled contract permits more than its source under 24 source mutations. In 770 agent sessions, SkillCFI blocks before dispatch all 240 such violations, which an allowlist admits, and normal tasks complete nearly as often as without it. Listing the next legal steps in a refusal raises recovery from 21% to 65%. Checking takes about 2% of task time, and a compact command form cuts session slowdown from 1.32 times to 1.08 times. None of 53 public skills is accepted as written. The compiler's diagnostics point to interfaces rather than workflows and guided seven into enforceable contracts.

Cryptography and Security.title: PULSAR-V: I/O-Aware Post-Update Attestation for RISC-V
Cryptography and Security.summary: Post-update attestation proves that a device installed the intended firmware, not that the image stayed protected until the report was signed. In a multi-master SoC, a master outside the attested processor can corrupt update-critical memory. In contrast, the firmware identity, lifecycle state, and the CPU's protection evidence remain byte-identical to a healthy device's. We present PULSAR-V, a post-update attestation architecture which binds the authenticated update commit to the effective permissions and immutability of both gates (PMP/EPMP on the CPU, the I/O policy mediating DMA), sampled at the commit and at attestation, the I/O gate latching its own commit-time state in hardware. In a RISC-V SoC prototyped on a ZCU102 FPGA (CV32E40S core with 16 PMP regions, IOPMP-style unit, AXI write guard), a 256-byte write from the board's Arm DMA engine bypasses PMP and corrupts the committed image: every conventional claim stays true, and PULSAR-V rejects the device on its I/O-policy evidence alone. It also rejects an intact device whose policy left the image writable, a verdict no integrity check can reach. The gate and its commit latch cost 436 LUTs, 4.6% of the SoC, and evidence collection takes 43.1k cycles independent of image size, 41x less than re-hashing 16 KiB.

Cryptography and Security.title: Evaluating LIM Trading Agents: A Critical Review of Backtesting Validity and Reporting Practices
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in investment research, and many studies report promising historical returns. However, such results are only credible if researchers can demonstrate that the model used only information available at the time, account for how strategies and configurations were selected, and explain how reported returns were generated. We identify six common threats to validity in LLM investment evaluations and apply them to 18 published studies. Across 108 assessments, we find substantial gaps in reporting. No paper fully addresses information timing, model-memory exposure, universe selection, trading costs, or configuration-selection bias. Only four studies provide minimum evidence that results hold across multiple market periods.
